title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Hyperscale shuts down Bitcoin ops for a $1.2B AI deal in Dowagiac—plus the bigger fight over local control and costs.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's Thursday, September 3, and yesterday a big shift happened out in Cass County that ties right into the fights we've been tracking all summer.
Yeah, Hyperscale Data just flipped the switch on its Dowagiac site from Bitcoin mining to AI compute.
Exactly. They shut down all the miners effective September 1 under a master services agreement that could bring in 1.2 billion dollars, with options pushing toward 3 billion.
And they're only using about 20 percent of the site's eventual 340 megawatt capacity. So this feels like the start of something bigger.
It does. The company is reallocating power that was going to crypto hashing over to AI workloads for a California neocloud customer. First 20 megawatts online later this year, with room to scale.
Graham, walk me through why this pivot matters beyond just one company. We've seen Michigan towns wrestling with these projects for months now.

Well, this site in Dowagiac has been a Bitcoin operation for a while, and the shift shows how the economics are changing fast. AI contracts look steadier and higher margin than mining, especially with long-term deals like this one.
But the power demands are still massive. A gigawatt-scale campus uses as much electricity as a small city. How does that hit regular ratepayers?
That's the core concern. Utilities like Consumers Energy are already upgrading infrastructure in places like West Michigan to handle surging loads from data centers and other big users.
And we know from other stories that new rules could limit the tax abatements towns have used to attract these projects. If those breaks shrink, do residents end up paying more locally?
That's what the proposed state bill aims to address. It would cap local tax incentives that developers have relied on, which could mean higher property taxes or fewer sweeteners for communities.
At the same time, Congressman John James has been vocal lately pushing for local control, even though his past votes went the other way on letting cities decide.
Right, a new report shows he voted four times against measures that would have given more say to townships. Now he's arguing communities should set their own rules.

That tension is playing out everywhere. Look at Washtenaw County, where the University of Michigan is moving ahead with a billion-dollar nuclear research facility in Ypsilanti despite local pushback, much like the OpenAI-related project in Saline.
And in Ionia, residents got their first public look yesterday at the power and water risks before any formal proposals even land. They're trying to get ahead of it.

St. Clair County has a workshop coming up on health impacts like noise, air, and water strain. These meetings are happening because people 30 or 60 miles away are starting to connect the dots on grid pressure and groundwater.
Exactly. A township in Oakland County is also heading to court to defend its rejection of a power-hungry campus, and another city says new zoning rules have already killed a developer's lawsuit.

So the Hyperscale move in Cass County is part of this larger wave. The site was already there for mining, but converting it to AI keeps the power demand and adds the cooling needs that come with high-performance compute.
And with Michigan having more local moratoriums than any other state right now, developers are looking for sites that are already permitted or easier to adapt.
What happens next for Dowagiac specifically? The company has said it might keep some mining in Montana, but Michigan is clearly the focus for the AI transition.

They plan to retrofit sections of the 617,000-square-foot campus and have already bought adjacent land. The initial deal taps 20 megawatts now, with options for more, all while the full site could eventually hit 340 megawatts.
That scale is what worries folks in places like Ionia or St. Clair. Even 20 percent of capacity is a lot of load on the grid.
And it ties directly into those tax break debates. If the new bill passes, future projects might not get the same abatements that helped lure this one.
Residents could see higher local taxes or just fewer incentives overall. Meanwhile, the power and water questions remain front and center.
We've heard from multiple communities that data centers can strain drinking supplies and push up rates if the utility has to build new generation or lines.
So is this pivot a sign that AI is the future here, or just one company's move while others keep pushing crypto or mixed uses?
It looks like a broader trend. The revenue numbers on these AI contracts are drawing companies away from volatile mining toward steady colocation deals.
And with 19 or more townships already paused, the next wave of projects will face even tighter scrutiny on zoning and resources.
That's why the Ionia meeting and the St. Clair workshop matter. They're giving residents a chance to shape rules early.
Graham, how many of these sites are we talking about statewide right now?
At least a dozen proposals in various stages, from West Michigan to southeast counties, with big names like Google and others evaluating spots.
And the Consumers Energy work on Cherry Street is one example of the grid upgrades already underway to keep up.
West Michigan customers might see more construction and, down the line, rate impacts tied to that demand growth.
Putting it together, the Hyperscale shift shows the industry adapting, but the local fights over control, costs, and resources are only heating up.
We'll keep watching how the state bill on tax breaks moves and what the court cases in Oakland and elsewhere decide.
Now let's hit the other stories from yesterday quickly.

First up, that state bill limiting tax abatements for new data centers. Towns have used those breaks to compete for jobs and investment, but if it passes, locals could face higher taxes or fewer incentives.
And the report on Congressman James voting against local control measures four times before. Voters in competitive districts might weigh that in the midterms.
In Washtenaw, the University of Michigan is pressing ahead with its Ypsilanti project over community objections, echoing the Saline pattern.
A city is arguing its updated zoning makes a developer's lawsuit over a blocked project moot. The outcome could decide if the company restarts or drops it.
Ionia residents got an early briefing on power and water risks yesterday, even before proposals arrive. Smart move for a community 30 miles from potential sites.
An Oakland County township is asking a judge to toss a developer's suit after rejecting a big campus. The ruling could set precedent for other communities.
St. Clair County has a public session coming on noise, air, and water health risks from proposed centers.
And Rep. James is now pushing local control, which contrasts with his earlier federal votes.
Finally, Consumers Energy started Cherry Street upgrades tied to rising loads from data centers and others.
Those are the quick hits. Now, on deck for listeners who want to weigh in.
Ionia's proactive meeting already happened, but St. Clair County's workshop on health impacts is coming up soon.
And keep an eye on any follow-up sessions in Oakland or Washtenaw as those court and university projects develop.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.
